title: Why is one cup of filter coffee stronger than another?
description: Regular, strong and light filter coffee are compared by how much decoction goes with each millilitre of milk. The fractions are put over a common denominator to see which is more. Keeko's doubt is that more decoction always means stronger coffee.
teaching_notes: One idea: coffee is stronger when it has more decoction for the same amount of milk, so we compare the two amounts together. Watch for students who compare only the decoction.

source: Regular filter coffee is 15 mL decoction to 35 mL milk, stro
video_script.why: The child uses ratios to compare mixtures with different amounts of both parts, which one amount alone cannot do.
video_script.substitution: Divide the decoction by the milk for each cup and compare the fractions.
video_script.anchor: Laksh's coffee shop: three cups of regular, strong and light filter coffee
video_script.wrong_move: Keeko says more decoction means stronger. Twenty millilitres of decoction in sixty millilitres of milk has more decoction than the regular cup but a smaller fraction, so the bubble is struck.
video_script.payoff_line: Strong coffee has more decoction for each millilitre of milk, and light coffee has less.

final_answer.value: Strong: 2/3 is more than 3/7; light: 1/4 is less than 3/7
final_answer.spoken: strong coffee has more decoction for each millilitre of milk, two thirds against three sevenths, and light coffee has less, one quarter

video_script.fraction_reading: three sevenths, two thirds, one quarter, one third

names.Laksh: runs the coffee shop and mixes regular, strong and light filter coffee

hold_back: Answer: strong coffee has more decoction
maths_rules: regular: 15 mL decoction to 35 mL milk; simplest form 3 : 7; decoction for each mL of milk 15 ÷ 35 = 3/7
strong: 20 mL to 30 mL; simplest form 2 : 3; decoction for each mL of milk 20 ÷ 30 = 2/3
light: 10 mL to 40 mL; simplest form 1 : 4; decoction for each mL of milk 10 ÷ 40 = 1/4
strong against regular: 3/7 = 9/21 and 2/3 = 14/21; 14/21 is more than 9/21
light against regular: 3/7 = 12/28 and 1/4 = 7/28; 7/28 is less than 12/28
Keeko's slip, illustration: 20 mL decoction with 60 mL milk; 20 ÷ 60 = 1/3 = 7/21, which is less than 3/7 = 9/21, though 20 is more than 15
video_script.design: One idea: compare the decoction for each millilitre of milk. Assumes ratios and fractions over a common denominator. Wrong idea: more decoction always means stronger. The three cups stay for the whole video.
open_questions: The Keeko illustration uses 20 mL of decoction with 60 mL of milk, which is not in the book; it is used only to break the doubt.

narration: <bookmark mark='r'/>Step one, take regular coffee and divide the decoction by the milk.
<bookmark mark='d'/>Fifteen divided by thirty five is three sevenths.
<bookmark mark='s'/>Step two, for strong coffee, twenty divided by thirty is two thirds.
<bookmark mark='l'/>For light coffee, ten divided by forty is one quarter.

narration: <bookmark mark='den'/>Step three, compare strong with regular over twenty one.
Three sevenths is nine twenty firsts, and two thirds is fourteen twenty firsts.
<bookmark mark='more'/>Fourteen is more than nine, so strong has more decoction for the same milk.

marks.den: both fractions are written with denominator 28: 3/7 = 12/28 and 1/4 = 7/28

narration: <bookmark mark='den'/>Step four, compare light with regular over twenty eight.
Three sevenths is twelve twenty eighths, and one quarter is seven twenty eighths.
<bookmark mark='less'/>Seven is less than twelve, so light has less decoction for the same milk.

narration: <bookmark mark='doubt'/>Keeko thinks more decoction means stronger.
<bookmark mark='more'/>Twenty millilitres is more than fifteen millilitres.
<bookmark mark='mug'/>But picture twenty millilitres of decoction in sixty millilitres of milk.
<bookmark mark='fix'/>Twenty divided by sixty is one third, which is seven twenty firsts.
<bookmark mark='frac'/>That is less than nine twenty firsts, so this cup is lighter than regular. We must look at the milk too.
